From Stone to Screen

A visual timeline of writing and typography

From Stone to Screen

Five thousand years ago, someone pressed a reed into wet clay so a stranger could read it later. Every chapter since has changed the tool and kept the job. This is the story of how language got a body: glyphs, mediums, inks, machines, and finally pixels that move.

26 chapters. Tap a chip for the detail behind each date. All photographs are public domain or Creative Commons, credited in place.

01 / 26 Before writing

Before writing

c. 20,000 BCIshango, Congo

Counting before words

Before anyone wrote a word, people carved marks that meant something. The Ishango bone carries grouped tally notches cut around twenty thousand years ago. It is not writing. There is no language in it. But it is the first surviving habit of the hand that writing would later depend on: pressing meaning into a durable surface so that someone else, later, can read it back.

Ancient scripts

c. 3200 BCUruk, Sumer

The first writing

Writing begins with accountants. In the city of Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, temple administrators needed to track grain, beer, and sheep, and the tokens and pictures they used hardened into a system: cuneiform, wedge shapes pressed into wet clay with a cut reed. Within centuries it could record not just inventory but law, prayer, and literature, including the epic of Gilgamesh. The medium mattered. Fired clay is nearly indestructible, which is why hundreds of thousands of tablets survive.

Ancient scripts

c. 1275 BCThebes, Egypt

Hieroglyphs and papyrus

Egypt gave writing two things at once: a script of extraordinary visual ambition and the first great portable medium. Hieroglyphs appear by about 3100 BC, carved in stone for eternity. For daily use, scribes wrote cursive hieratic with reed pens on papyrus, sheets pressed from Nile reeds, using black ink made of soot and gum and red ink of ocher. The scribe Hunefer commissioned this Book of the Dead around 1275 BC. The ink is still black after three thousand years.

Ancient scripts

c. 1200 BCAnyang, China

Oracle bones

The earliest Chinese writing we can read was addressed to the future in the most literal way: questions for ancestors and gods, carved on ox scapulae and turtle shells, then cracked with heat so diviners could read the answers. Royal diviners at the Shang court recorded the question, sometimes the answer, and sometimes whether it came true. More than three thousand years later, the script on these bones is recognizably the ancestor of the Chinese characters used today, the oldest writing system still in continuous use.

Ancient scripts

c. 1000 BCByblos, Phoenicia

The alphabet jump

Cuneiform had hundreds of signs. Egyptian had more. The decisive compression came on the Levantine coast: a set of roughly twenty-two letters standing not for things or syllables but for consonant sounds. With the Phoenician alphabet, literacy no longer required a scribal career; a trader could learn the system in weeks. The Greeks borrowed it and added vowels. The Romans borrowed it from the Greeks. Nearly every alphabet in use today, Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, descends from this one invention.

Ancient scripts

196 BCRosetta, Egypt

One decree, three scripts

A granodiorite slab carrying a priestly decree of 196 BC in three scripts became, by accident, the key to an entire civilization. Found by French soldiers near Rosetta in 1799 and surrendered to Britain in 1801, the stone let scholars compare known Greek against lost Egyptian. Jean-Francois Champollion announced the decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822, reading the cartouche of Ptolemy sound by sound. A dead script came back to life, and with it fifteen hundred years of silenced text.

Ancient scripts

AD 113Rome

Roman capitals

At the base of Trajan's Column in Rome, cut in AD 113, stands the inscription that typographers still treat as a benchmark. The letters were brush-drawn first, then carved, and the chisel following the brush left flared stroke endings: serifs. The proportions of capitalis monumentalis, the wide O, the narrow E, the balanced M, became the model for capital letters in the Latin world. When type designers in the twentieth century needed a classical capital, they went back to this stone and measured it.

Scrolls to books

c. 125 BCQumran, Judea

Scrolls and carbon ink

For a thousand years the book was a roll. The Great Isaiah Scroll, copied around 125 BC and found in a cave at Qumran in 1947, runs more than seven meters: fifty-four columns of Hebrew on seventeen stitched sheets of parchment. The ink is carbon black, soot bound in gum, the same chemistry as Egypt. Scrolls demanded sequence; you read them in order, winding as you went. The codex, pages bound at a spine, would replace the roll partly because it let readers jump.

Scrolls to books

Han dynasty onwardChina

Brush, ink, paper, inkstone

Chinese writing built its own complete toolchain, honored as the Four Treasures of the Study: the flexible hair brush, the ink stick of pine soot and animal glue, the inkstone for grinding it with water, and paper. Where the Roman world wrote with rigid pens, the brush made every stroke a gesture with thick and thin built in. Calligraphy became the highest visual art of East Asia, and the aesthetics of the brushstroke shaped how Chinese characters are judged, taught, and designed to this day.

Scrolls to books

AD 105Luoyang, China

Paper

In AD 105 the Han court official Cai Lun presented the emperor with a recipe: macerate bark, hemp waste, old rags, and fishing nets into pulp, lift a thin layer on a screen, press and dry it. Paper was cheaper than silk and lighter than bamboo strips, and it spread with Chinese administration and Buddhist copying. The technology moved west slowly, reaching Samarkand by the eighth century, Baghdad by 793, Moorish Spain by the eleventh century, and Italy by the thirteenth. Europe printed on a Chinese invention.

Printing

AD 868Dunhuang, China

The first printed book

Printing did not begin with Gutenberg. The Diamond Sutra found in the cave library at Dunhuang is a complete woodblock-printed scroll with a colophon dating it precisely: the 13th day of the 4th moon of the 9th year of Xiantong, that is, May 11, 868. Its frontispiece is confident, detailed, and clearly the product of a mature craft. Whole pages were carved in relief on wooden blocks, inked, and rubbed onto paper. For texts in thousands of characters, block printing suited Chinese perfectly.

Printing

1377Cheongju, Korea

Metal movable type

Movable type was invented twice. Bi Sheng made type of baked clay in China around 1040, and Korea perfected casting type in bronze. The Jikji, an anthology of Zen Buddhist teachings printed at Heungdeok temple in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type. Korea even reformed its writing to fit: King Sejong's hangul alphabet of 1443 was designed from scratch for easy learning. What Korea lacked was not technology but Gutenberg's commercial print market.

Scribes

c. 800Iona and Kells

The illuminated page

While print gestated in Asia, European monks pushed the handwritten page toward the condition of jewelry. The Book of Kells, a gospel book made by Columban monks around 800, turns the opening letters of Christ's name into a full page of spirals, knots, animals, and angels. Its script, insular majuscule, is itself a designed object: regular, round, and legible across a dark church. Medieval scriptoria standardized letterforms centuries before type did, because a scriptorium is a factory for consistent writing.

Scribes

1400sBurgundy

The scribe at work

This is the system Gutenberg disrupted, pictured from inside: Jean Mielot, professional scribe to Philip the Good of Burgundy, at a sloped desk with quill, knife, inkhorn, and exemplar. A quill is a goose feather cut with a penknife; iron gall ink is made from oak galls, iron salts, and gum, and it bites into parchment rather than sitting on top. A single Bible took a scribe roughly a year or more. Copying was slow, expensive, and introduced errors with every generation. Demand for books was outrunning the hand.

Print revolution

c. 1455Mainz, Germany

Gutenberg

Johannes Gutenberg's genius was integration. Around Mainz in the early 1450s he combined the adjustable hand mold for casting type in a lead, tin, and antimony alloy, an oil-based ink sticky enough for metal, and a converted screw press. The 42-line Bible, finished around 1455 in an edition of roughly 180 copies, matched the density and blackness of the best scribal work. Within fifty years, presses in over 250 European towns had printed many millions of books. The price of the written word collapsed, and everything downstream of cheap text, the Reformation, modern science, the newspaper, became possible.

Print revolution

1530sParis and Venice

The punchcutters

Every piece of type began as a steel punch, a letter carved in mirror image on the end of a hard steel bar, by eye, at final size. The punchcutters were the first type designers. Nicolas Jenson in Venice cut the roman that ended blackletter's dominance in 1470. Aldus Manutius published compact classics that made books portable. And in Paris, Claude Garamont cut romans of such balance that revivals of his letters, under the name Garamond, are still among the most used book faces five centuries later.

Print revolution

1734London

The specimen sheet

By the eighteenth century, type was an industry with marketing. William Caslon's 1734 broadside specimen displayed his romans, italics, and exotics in graded sizes, a single sheet that said: here is everything we sell. The specimen formalized the idea of a type family, one design across many sizes, and typefounders competed on it. Caslon's sturdy letters set the Declaration of Independence's first printing. After him, John Baskerville sharpened contrast and smoothed paper, and Giambattista Bodoni in Parma pushed stroke contrast to the edge of dazzle.

Industrial age

1800sEverywhere

Type by the ton

For four hundred years after Gutenberg, every page was still assembled by hand, letter by letter, from cases like this one, by compositors reading mirror writing at speed. The nineteenth century industrialized everything around them. Friedrich Koenig's steam-driven cylinder press printed The Times of London on November 29, 1814, at over 1,100 sheets an hour. Paper went from rag to wood pulp in the 1840s. Aniline and industrial pigment chemistry replaced soot recipes. Rotary presses fed by paper rolls made the mass-circulation newspaper, and with it mass literacy, an everyday fact.

Industrial age

1886New York

The Linotype

Hand composition was the bottleneck, and Ottmar Mergenthaler, a German-born mechanic in Baltimore, broke it. His Linotype, first used at the New York Tribune in 1886, let an operator type at a keyboard while the machine assembled brass matrices, justified the line with sliding wedges, and cast it as a single slug of hot metal, then redistributed the matrices automatically. One operator did the work of several hand compositors. Thomas Edison reportedly called it the eighth wonder of the world. Big city dailies swelled from eight pages to forty-eight, and the profession of hot-metal operator lasted ninety years.

Into the machine

1949Brooklyn, NY

Type becomes light

After five hundred years, type stopped being a thing you could drop on your foot. The Intertype Fotosetter, demonstrated in the late 1940s and built in Brooklyn, kept the hot-metal mechanics but swapped the caster for a camera: letters became images on film negatives, flashed onto photographic paper. By the 1960s and 70s, cathode ray tube machines like the Linotron set thousands of characters per second. Photo lettering also loosened the rules. Letters could overlap, stretch, and touch, and 1970s design reveled in it. Herb Lubalin's tight, expressive headlines were only possible on film.

Into the machine

1890 to 1963United States

Text as data

Computers met the alphabet through holes in cardboard. Herman Hollerith's punched cards tabulated the 1890 US census, and IBM's 80-column card became the unit of machine-readable text for decades, one line per card, uppercase only. The real milestone was agreeing what the holes meant. In 1963, the ASCII standard assigned numbers to 128 characters: A is 65, a is 97, space is 32. For the first time, a letter had a universal numeric identity independent of any physical form. Every font, email, and web page since is a way of drawing numbers.

Into the machine

1978Maynard, Massachusetts

The glowing grid

On a terminal like the DEC VT100, text became ephemeral for the first time in its history: letters of glowing phosphor, redrawn sixty times a second, gone when the power dropped. The VT100 displayed 80 columns, the punched card's ghost, of fixed-width characters drawn from a ROM as tiny dot grids. Every glyph occupied an identical cell, which is why the era's letters look the way they do. Its escape codes for cursor control became an ANSI standard that terminal emulators still honor today, half a century later.

Into the machine

1982Everywhere, 8 bits at a time

8-bit letters

The home computers of the early 1980s put a character set in millions of living rooms. The Commodore 64, the best-selling computer model of all time, drew every letter on an 8 by 8 pixel grid, 2K of ROM holding the whole alphabet, plus the card suits and box-drawing shapes of PETSCII. Designing a legible lowercase e in 64 pixels is a brutal typographic discipline, and the people who did it were doing type design whether anyone called it that or not. The blocky look they could not avoid became a style people now choose on purpose.

Personal type

1984Cupertino, California

Type for everyone

The 1984 Macintosh made type a consumer choice. Steve Jobs, who had audited a calligraphy class at Reed College after dropping out, insisted the Mac ship with proportionally spaced fonts, and Susan Kare drew them: Chicago, Geneva, Monaco, bitmap families designed pixel by pixel. For the first time, ordinary people chose typefaces from a menu. The next year completed the revolution: Adobe's PostScript described letters as mathematical outlines, printable at any size, and the Apple LaserWriter plus Aldus PageMaker put a print shop on a desk. Desktop publishing gutted the typesetting industry within a decade.

Personal type

1990CERN, Geneva

Text that links

On a NeXT machine at CERN in 1990, Tim Berners-Lee wrote a program for text that points at other text, and writing changed again. A web page is not a fixed artifact like a printed sheet; it reflows to fit whatever screen it lands on, styled by rules the reader's machine interprets. For its first fifteen years the web could only use fonts the reader already had, a dozen so-called web-safe faces. The @font-face rule, finally practical around 2009 and 2010, let pages ship their own type. Within a few years services like Google Fonts were serving billions of font files a day, and the whole history of type design was suddenly a dropdown.

Now

2016 and onwardYour screen

Type that moves

In 2016, Apple, Google, Microsoft, and Adobe jointly announced OpenType variable fonts: a single file holding a whole design space, with weight, width, slant, and anything else the designer defines as continuous axes. A letterform is no longer a fixed thing but a point in a space of possibilities, and it can move. Interfaces now animate type in response to touch, scroll, and attention. The glyph below is live; it is being computed as you interact with it. Five thousand years after a reed pressed a wedge into clay, writing has become software, and the surface finally writes back.
